analogy.p: A histogram is like a map of population density. The number of people living in a region equals the density (people per square kilometre) times the area of the region. A small region with a high density can hold as many people as a large region with a low density, just as a narrow tall bar can have the same area as a wide short bar. Frequency density is the density and the class width is the length of the region on the number line. The analogy breaks down because a map region has two dimensions, whereas a histogram class has one dimension (width on the x-axis) with the second dimension (height) being the density itself, so the 'area' is a representation rather than a real land area.

bullets: A histogram is used for **continuous** data grouped into classes; a bar chart is used for **discrete or categorical** data (colours, number of pets, etc.).
In a histogram the **bars touch** because there are no gaps in a continuous scale; in a bar chart there are gaps.
The key rule is **area of bar = frequency** (or, when equal widths are used, area is proportional to frequency).
When all class widths are equal, the height can be frequency, but with **unequal widths** the vertical axis must be **frequency density**.
The vertical axis of a histogram is therefore labelled **Frequency density**, never just 'Frequency' (unless every class has the same width).
The horizontal axis is a **continuous number scale** with a label and units, and class boundaries are marked on it, not class labels written between the bars.
A histogram shows the **shape of a distribution**: where the data is concentrated (the tallest bar is the **modal class**), how spread out it is, and whether it is symmetric or skewed.
Link: the same grouped data can also be shown in a frequency polygon, a cumulative frequency graph or a box plot, but only a histogram shows the distribution by area.
core.h: What a histogram is and how it differs from a bar chart
core.p: A **histogram** is a diagram for **continuous grouped data** (such as time, mass, length or age) in which the **area of each bar is proportional to the frequency** of that class. Because the bars represent a continuous scale, they **touch with no gaps**, and the horizontal axis is a proper number line. This is different from a bar chart, where bars have equal widths, gaps between them, and it is the height that shows frequency. On the Edexcel Higher paper you must be able to draw and interpret histograms **with unequal class widths**, which is where the idea of frequency density becomes essential.

bullets: **Frequency density** = frequency ÷ class width. It tells you the frequency **per unit** of the variable (for example people per minute).
Bars of different widths cannot be compared by frequency alone; **frequency density corrects for width**.
Using frequency density makes the **area** of each bar equal to the frequency, which is the defining property of a histogram.
If a wide class and a narrow class have the same frequency, the wide class has the **smaller** frequency density, so its bar is **shorter**.
If you plotted frequency instead of FD with unequal widths, the wide classes would look far too big: this is the commonest error in drawing histograms.
Think of it as 'people per minute': a class with 40 people over 10 minutes has density 4, but 40 people over 20 minutes only has density 2.
The units of frequency density depend on the data: for example **people per minute** or **plants per cm**.
Statistics link: this is the same idea as population density, which is people per square kilometre rather than total people in a region.
core.p: Imagine two classes of data: 0 to 10 minutes and 10 to 30 minutes. If both contain 40 people, the second class is twice as wide, so those 40 people are spread over a bigger range and are **less crowded**. If we drew bars of height 40 for both, the wide bar would look twice as big and give a misleading impression that there are more people in it. **Frequency density** solves this by measuring **how crowded the data is per one unit on the x-axis**, so that equal areas always represent equal frequencies.

bullets: **Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width** (used when DRAWING a histogram from a table).
**Frequency = frequency density × class width** (used when READING a histogram to find how many are in a class).
**Class width = upper class boundary − lower class boundary**; for 20 < t ≤ 30 the width is 30 − 20 = 10.
Frequency is also the **area of the bar** = width × height, because height is frequency density.
Worked example of the idea: frequency 30, width 20: FD = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5; check: 1.5 × 20 = 30.
If the question says 'the bar has height 3 and width 5', frequency = 3 × 5 = 15, but **only if the vertical axis is frequency density**.
Always check your answer by multiplying back: FD × width should return the original frequency.
The **total frequency** is the sum of all the bar areas, so totals can be found from the histogram too.
core.p: Everything in this topic comes from one relationship: **frequency density = frequency ÷ class width**. Rearranging it gives the other two formulae you need: **frequency = frequency density × class width** and **class width = frequency ÷ frequency density**. The second one is the most used in exams because you are often given a drawn histogram and asked for the frequency of a class, or the height of a bar and asked for a frequency. Always write out which formula you are using, because method marks are given for the correct substitution.

bullets: Write classes with inequalities, such as **10 < t ≤ 20**; the value 10 belongs to the **previous** class and 20 belongs to this one.
Class width is **upper boundary − lower boundary**, not the number of whole values in the class.
If data is given as rounded values (for example 'lengths measured to the nearest cm: 10 to 19'), convert to real boundaries first (9.5 to 19.5) before finding the width.
The x-axis must show the **class boundaries** (the ends of the bars), not the midpoints.
Classes can be of **different widths**: for example, wider classes where data is sparse and narrower classes where it is dense.
Open-ended classes (such as 'over 80') cannot be drawn in a histogram unless an upper limit is given or assumed.
The sum of all the bar areas equals the total number of observations, which is a useful check on a drawn histogram.
Link to cumulative frequency: the same upper class boundaries are used on the x-axis there.
core.p: For continuous data, classes are written using inequalities, for example **0 < t ≤ 10** means t is greater than 0 and at most 10. The **class boundaries** are the numbers at the ends of each class (0, 10, 20, 30, 50 and 80 in the example). The class width is found by subtracting the lower boundary from the upper boundary, and it is the width of the bar on the horizontal axis. Because one class ends exactly where the next begins, there are no gaps and the bars touch.

bullets: **Step 1:** Work out the class width of every class (upper boundary − lower boundary).
**Step 2:** Calculate **frequency density = frequency ÷ class width** for each class; keep decimals (for example 1.5, 0.5).
**Step 3:** Draw the axes: x-axis for the variable (with a continuous scale), y-axis for frequency density, both labelled with units.
**Step 4:** Choose a y-axis scale so the tallest bar fits and the scale uses equal steps (for example 0 to 6 in steps of 1).
**Step 5:** Draw each bar with the base from its lower boundary to its upper boundary and the height equal to the FD.
**Step 6:** Make sure bars **touch** each other and use a ruler; check that the widths match the class widths.
Write the FD values on the table or on the bars so the examiner can see them.
Check: add up (FD × width) for all bars to see if you get the total frequency.
If the question gives a histogram scale such as '1 cm² represents 5 people', work in areas instead (see the scale-problem section).
core.h: Drawing a histogram step by step
core.p: To draw a histogram from a grouped frequency table, work through a fixed routine. First add a column for class width, then a column for frequency density, then choose suitable scales and draw touching bars. The routine is the same every time and marks are awarded for each stage, so showing the working in a table is the safest way to earn them. A typical question gives you a table with some frequency densities missing and asks you to complete it and draw the histogram.

bullets: The y-axis starts at **0** and is labelled **Frequency density** (and, if helpful, with units such as 'people per minute').
Use **equal steps** on each axis; for FD values with halves (1.5, 0.5) a step of 0.5 or 1 per large square is most practical.
Choose a scale so the tallest bar uses most of the grid; do not make the histogram tiny.
On the x-axis, mark each **class boundary**, even where the widths differ, so the bars line up with the scale.
If the graph already has axes drawn, you may be told the first bar's height (frequency density) and have to find the scale from that.
Label axes with the **quantity and units** (for example 'Time (minutes)').
A common method mark: 'at least 3 bars correct' or 'bars touching with correct widths'; do each bar carefully.
Always leave bars unshaded or lightly shaded; using different colours is unnecessary.
core.p: Marks for drawing a histogram include correct axes, labels and scales. The vertical axis must be labelled **Frequency density** and must start at zero, because the bars start at zero and the area has to be a true measure of the frequency. The horizontal axis is a number scale and can start at zero or at the lowest class boundary. Both axes should use the whole of the graph paper where possible, so the histogram is large and easy to read, and every scale must go up in equal steps.

bullets: Read the **height** of the bar from the vertical axis (check the scale on the grid: each small square may be 0.2, 0.5 or something else).
Read the **width** of the bar from the horizontal axis as upper boundary minus lower boundary.
**Frequency = height × width.** Example: class 30 to 50 with height 1.5 has frequency 1.5 × 20 = 30.
To find the **total** frequency, work out every bar area and add them up.
To find a **fraction or percentage** in a range, divide that frequency by the total (for example 40 out of 155 is 40/155 = 25.8%).
If the question asks 'how many more people are in this class than in that class', find both frequencies and subtract.
Do not just read the height as the frequency: that is the main mistake with histograms.
Where part of a bar is needed, see the next section.
core.p: To find the frequency in a class from a drawn histogram, **multiply the bar's height (frequency density) by its width**. The frequency of the whole class is the area of the bar. In an exam you are usually asked 'how many people took between 10 and 20 minutes?' and the answer is the area of that one bar. This is the opposite of drawing, so you use **frequency = frequency density × class width**. Always read the height from the vertical axis carefully by checking what each small square represents.

bullets: State the assumption: the data in each class is **evenly spread**.
For 15 to 25 minutes: the part of the 10–20 bar from 15 to 20 is 5 wide with FD 5, so 5 × 5 = 25.
The part of the 20–30 bar from 20 to 25 is 5 wide with FD 4, so 5 × 4 = 20.
Total = 25 + 20 = **45 people** (an estimate).
If the range lies inside one bar, just use width of the range × FD of that bar.
Many wasted marks occur by using the whole bar's frequency instead of the fraction of the bar.
You can also use fractions: 15 to 20 is half of the class 10 to 20, so half of 50 = 25.
The word **estimate** in the question is a signal to use this method.
core.h: Estimating from part of a class
core.p: A question may ask for the number of people with a time between, say, 15 and 25 minutes, where 15 and 25 are not class boundaries. You then **assume the data is spread evenly (uniformly) within each class**, so you can take the portion of the bar that lies in the range. The frequency in that part is the **height of the bar × the width of the part**. Add the parts from each bar. The answer is only an **estimate**, because the true spread inside a class is unknown, and you should say so in an exam.

bullets: Total frequency = **sum of (FD × width)** for all bars (155 in our example).
Proportion in a range = frequency in the range ÷ total frequency.
Probability that a randomly chosen value is in a range = proportion (give as fraction, decimal or percentage as asked).
Percentage = fraction × 100; make sure to give units and rounding as requested (for example 1 decimal place).
For 'more than' questions, you can find the frequency in the complementary range and subtract from the total.
For 'what fraction took less than 30 minutes?': 20 + 50 + 40 = 110 out of 155 = 110/155 = 22/31.
Always simplify fractions only if asked; otherwise a correct unsimplified fraction usually earns the mark.
Link: this is how histograms connect to probability and to relative frequency.
core.h: Totals, fractions and probabilities from a histogram
core.p: A histogram gives the whole distribution, so you can answer questions about **proportions** and **probabilities**. First find the total frequency by adding all the bar areas. Then the **proportion** in any range is that range's frequency divided by the total. If a person is chosen at random from the data, the **probability** they are in a range is the same fraction. These are often 2 or 3 mark questions combined with the estimation method from part of a class.

bullets: Find total frequency (155) and **half of it** (77.5). Quarters are 38.75 and 116.25.
Add the bar frequencies in order (cumulative): 20, then 70, then 110.
The median is in the **20 to 30** class because the running total passes 77.5 in that class.
The frequency still needed after 70 is 77.5 − 70 = 7.5; the FD of the class is 4.
The width needed is 7.5 ÷ 4 = 1.875, so the median is about 20 + 1.875 = **21.9 minutes**.
The same idea gives Q1 (38.75th value) in the 10 to 20 class: 18.75 more needed after 20, with FD 5, so 3.75 wide: Q1 ≈ 13.75.
State that the answer is an **estimate** because of the assumed even spread.
Link: this is the same value you would find from a cumulative frequency graph of the same data.
core.h: Estimating the median and quartiles from a histogram
core.p: The median is the middle value, which means the value below which **half of the total frequency** lies. In a histogram you find the median by working along the bars, **adding the areas** until you reach half the total, then working out how far into the bar you need to go. Because the data inside a class is assumed to be evenly spread, you can find the exact position inside the bar using width = frequency needed ÷ FD. The same method works for the lower and upper quartiles, using one quarter and three quarters of the total frequency.

bullets: **Modal class** = class with the **highest frequency density** (tallest bar): here 10 < t ≤ 20 (FD 5).
Do not choose the widest bar or the one with the largest area just because it looks big.
**Midpoint** = (lower boundary + upper boundary) ÷ 2: here 5, 15, 25, 40, 65.
Estimated mean = **Σ(midpoint × frequency) ÷ Σ frequency**.
Mean ≈ 4025 ÷ 155 = **26.0 minutes** (to 1 decimal place), an estimate because we used midpoints.
The mean (26.0) is larger than the median (21.9), which shows the distribution is **positively skewed** (a long tail to the right).
Link: see the Grouped data estimates topic for the same method with tables.
core.h: Estimating the mean and finding the modal class
core.p: The **modal class** of a histogram is the class with the **highest frequency density**, which is the **tallest bar**. It is not the class with the highest frequency, because the frequency depends on the width. To estimate the **mean** from the grouped data, you use the usual grouped method: take the midpoint of each class, multiply by its frequency, add them up and divide by the total frequency. With a histogram the frequencies first have to be found from the bar areas.

bullets: Frequency is **proportional to area** (width × height), so bar B's frequency = (area B ÷ area A) × frequency A.
Example: bar A is 10 wide and 3 cm tall (area 30) and represents 60 people; bar B is 20 wide and 2.5 cm tall (area 50) so it represents 60 × 50/30 = **100 people**.
Alternatively, find a scale: 60 people over a class width of 10 gives FD 6, which is 3 cm, so 1 cm represents FD 2.
The height of a bar is **frequency density**, so equal heights with different widths mean **different** frequencies.
A common instruction is 'the area of the 20–30 bar is 8 cm² and represents 40 people', so 1 cm² represents 5 people.
Check that your final frequencies add up to the stated total frequency.
Be careful with units: use the same unit of width on both bars (you can use the class width in minutes or in cm of the drawn scale).
Missing-bar problems: if the total frequency is given, subtract the other bars' frequencies to find the missing bar's frequency, then divide by its width to get its height.
core.h: Problems with no scale: using relative areas
core.p: Some questions show a histogram that has no frequency density axis values, but give you the frequency of one bar. You then use **proportion**: the frequency is proportional to the **area** of the bar, so frequencies can be compared through areas, or you can find the FD scale from the known bar. This type of question appears at grade 7 to 9 and tests whether you really understand that area, not height, represents frequency. Lay out the working in a small table of width, height, area and frequency.

bullets: Histogram: area = frequency; unequal widths allowed; y-axis = frequency density.
Frequency polygon: plot (midpoint, frequency) and join with straight lines; only works neatly with equal widths.
Cumulative frequency graph: plot (upper class boundary, cumulative frequency) and join with a smooth curve.
Box plot: shows minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum; ideal for comparing medians and spreads.
Bar chart: for discrete or categorical data with gaps between bars.
A histogram is best for showing the **shape** (skewed or symmetrical, one peak or two), while cumulative frequency is best for finding **averages and spreads**.
When comparing two histograms, refer to the **modal class** and the **spread** in context.
The data in a histogram can be turned into a cumulative frequency table by adding the bar areas.
core.p: Several diagrams can display the same grouped data, and exam questions often ask you to choose or compare. A **histogram** shows the distribution by area and handles unequal widths. A **frequency polygon** joins the midpoints of the tops of bars and is good for comparing two sets of data on one graph. A **cumulative frequency graph** shows running totals and is the tool for finding the median, quartiles and percentiles. A **box plot** summarises the five-number summary for quick comparisons.

bullets: Frequencies are counts, so they should come out as **whole numbers** (except for estimates from parts of classes).
Check that your bar areas add up to the stated total frequency.
Give a final answer with **units** and in context: '45 people' or '21.9 minutes'.
If a calculation gives a decimal frequency in a full class, you have probably misread the scale.
Label axes and give the graph a title if asked; use a ruler for all straight lines.
If asked to **comment** on a distribution, mention the modal class, the skew and any gap or outlier.
Look for words such as 'estimate', 'assume' and 'show that': these tell you what is expected in the answer.
Higher tier extension: you may need to combine the histogram with algebra (for example find an unknown frequency x from a histogram) or with probability.
core.h: Checking your work and common contexts
core.p: Examiners like to set histograms in everyday contexts: journey times, ages of people in a town, masses of apples, times taken to complete a puzzle. The mathematics is always the same, but you must give answers **in context**, with units. A good habit is to check each result for sense: frequencies should be whole numbers, the totals should match any given total, and a wide bar should usually not be as tall as a narrow bar unless it contains many more items.

exam: **1 mark** questions: ask for a frequency density or a bar height, or to complete one value in the table: show FD = f ÷ width, and give the number.
**2 mark** questions: 'Work out the number of people with a time between 10 and 20 minutes': 1 mark for height × width, 1 mark for the answer.
**3 mark** 'estimate' questions usually involve part of a class: 1 mark for the part width, 1 for multiplying by the FD, 1 for the final answer with the assumption.
**4 mark** questions combine drawing and calculation: complete the table (1 or 2 marks), draw the bars with correct widths (1 mark), correct heights (1 mark).
**5 or 6 mark** problem-solving questions combine a histogram with probability, a mean or the median: set out a table with width, FD, frequency and midpoint.

Command words: **'Draw'** means draw a histogram accurately with a ruler; **'Estimate'** means use an even-spread assumption; **'Work out'** means show a calculation; **'Show that'** needs every step.
Always write the formula (FD = frequency ÷ class width) before you substitute, so you earn the method mark even if you slip arithmetically.
On a drawn histogram, check the scale: find the value of one small square on the vertical axis before you read heights.
If the vertical axis is labelled 'Frequency' (not density) and all widths are equal, you can read heights as frequencies; check the widths first.
If asked to compare two distributions, give one comment about **average** (modal class or median) and one about **spread**, both in context.
Use a sharp pencil and a ruler; bars should be accurate to half a small square.
Round only at the end; keep at least 3 significant figures in working.

mistakes.r: Calculate frequency density = frequency ÷ class width and plot that, labelling the axis 'Frequency density'.
mistakes.w: Plotting frequency on the vertical axis when classes have unequal widths.

mistakes.r: Frequency = frequency density × class width (the area of the bar).
mistakes.w: Reading the height of a bar as the frequency.

mistakes.r: The bars touch because the data is continuous.
mistakes.w: Leaving gaps between the bars of a histogram.

mistakes.r: Multiply the width of the part by the frequency density, assuming an even spread.
mistakes.w: Using the whole bar's frequency when the question asks about a part of a class.

mistakes.r: The modal class is the class with the highest frequency density (the tallest bar).
mistakes.w: Choosing the widest or biggest-area bar as the modal class.

mistakes.r: The median is the value that splits the total frequency in half: add areas until you reach half the total.
mistakes.w: Finding the median as the middle of the x-axis range or the middle bar.

mistakes.r: Class width is the upper boundary minus the lower boundary: 50 − 20 = 30.
mistakes.w: Writing class widths from the labels, such as 10 for 'over 20 to 50'.

mistakes.r: Label the horizontal axis with the quantity and unit and the vertical axis 'Frequency density'.
mistakes.w: Not labelling the axes or leaving off the unit.

mistakes.r: Mark the class boundaries on the x-axis, not midpoints.
mistakes.w: Using the midpoints of the bars as the x-axis labels.

mistakes.r: State that you assume the data is spread evenly within each class and that the answer is an estimate.
mistakes.w: Giving an exact answer to an 'estimate' question without showing the assumption.

summary: You must be able to draw and interpret histograms for continuous grouped data, including those with unequal class widths, using frequency density = frequency ÷ class width so that the area of each bar represents the frequency. You also need to estimate frequencies, medians and means from a histogram, which is essential for the Edexcel Higher statistics questions.

terms.d: A diagram for continuous grouped data where the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency; bars touch.
Frequency divided by class width; the height of a bar in a histogram.
The upper class boundary minus the lower class boundary.
The value at the end of a class where one class stops and the next begins.
Data that can take any value within a range, such as time, mass or height.
The class with the highest frequency density (the tallest bar in a histogram).
The value halfway between the lower and upper boundaries of a class.
An approximate answer found by assuming data is evenly spread within each class.
The lack of symmetry in a distribution; positive skew has a long tail to the right.
The number of observations that fall in a class.
The sum of all the frequencies; the sum of all bar areas.
A diagram for discrete or categorical data with equal width bars separated by gaps; the height shows the frequency.
A running total of frequencies up to the upper boundary of each class.
The middle value; the value that half the data lies below.
The fraction of the data in a given range; frequency in the range divided by the total.

worked.ans: Frequency densities (bar heights): 2, 5, 4, 1.5, 0.5, all labelled on the vertical axis 'Frequency density'.
worked.q: The table shows the times (t minutes) taken by 155 people to complete a puzzle. Complete the table with the frequency density and state the height of each bar of the histogram. 0<t≤10: 20, 10<t≤20: 50, 20<t≤30: 40, 30<t≤50: 30, 50<t≤80: 15. [3 marks]
steps: Use frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.

worked.ans: About 80 people (an estimate, assuming an even spread within each class).
worked.q: Use the histogram to estimate the number of people who took between 15 and 40 minutes. [3 marks]
steps: Assume the times are spread evenly within each class.
15 to 20 (part of the 10–20 bar): width 5, FD 5, so 5 × 5 = 25.
30 to 40 (part of the 30–50 bar): width 10, FD 1.5, so 10 × 1.5 = 15.

worked.q: In a different histogram, the bar for 10<x≤20 has height 3 cm and represents 60 people. The bar for 20<x≤40 has height 2.5 cm. How many people does it represent? [3 marks]
steps: The vertical axis is frequency density, so for the first bar FD = 60 ÷ 10 = 6, which is 3 cm. So 1 cm represents an FD of 2.
